Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a real-time scene at the ferry landing, utilizing concrete actions, sensory details (the cold metal, the clicking suitcase handle, the rain), and sparse, realistic dialogue to build quiet tension between Ilse and Jonas. Rather than interrupting the pacing with heavy blocks of exposition, the author seamlessly weaves brief moments of summary and backstory directly into the scene—such as Ilse's memory of Jonas refusing to wear a hood in the rain, the past tension with Henning at the kitchen table, and the routine of the impatient delivery driver on Thursdays. This delicate integration provides all the necessary context about their strained mother-son relationship and the setting without ever pulling the reader out of the immediate moment.
